'''Sundquist:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}}
'''Bredesen:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Ned McWherter]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Don Sundquist]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | turnout = 56.62%{{Cite news |date=November 8, 1994 |title=Tennessee Voter Turnout in 1994 |work=Tennessee Secretary of State |url=https://sos.tn.gov/elections/statistics |access-date=April 17, 2023 |archive-url= |archive-date=}} }} {{ElectionsTN}} The '''1994 Tennessee gubernatorial election''' took place on November 8, 1994 to elect the next [[governor of Tennessee]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Ned McWherter]] was term-limited, leaving the governorship an open seat. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] congressman [[Don Sundquist]] was elected [[Governor of Tennessee]], defeating Democratic nominee [[Phil Bredesen]], the mayor of [[Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]], who later won Tennessee's governorship in [[2002 Tennessee gubernatorial election|2002]] & [[2006 Tennessee gubernatorial election|2006]]. == Campaign == Democratic candidate [[Phil Bredesen]] criticized Republican candidate [[Don Sundquist]] for voting against a [[Minimum wage in the United States|minimum wage]] increase while voting for a congressional pay raise. Sundquist accused Bredesen of [[Flip-flop (politics)|flip-flopping]] on issues such as public funding for abortion and school privatization.Phillip Langsdon, ''Tennessee: A Political History'' (Franklin, Tenn.: Hillsboro Press, 2000), pp. 408–412. == Aftermath == [[Don Sundquist]] focused on government efficiency and [[welfare reform]].Carroll Van West, "[http://tennesseeencyclopedia.net/entry.php?rec=1285 Don Sundquist]," ''Tennessee Encyclopedia of History and Culture'', 2009. Retrieved: January 9, 2013. He signed the "Families First" bill in 1996, which reduced the number of families on welfare from 70,000 to 30,000.[http://www.nga.org/cms/home/governors/past-governors-bios/page_tennessee/col2-content/main-content-list/title_sundquist_don.html Don Sundquist], National Governors Association website. Retrieved: January 9, 2013. {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130612194923/https://www.nga.org/cms/home/governors/past-governors-bios/page_tennessee/col2-content/main-content-list/title_sundquist_don.html|date=June 12, 2013}} He also signed a series of crime-related measures which called for tougher sentences and more focus on victims' rights.Carroll Van West, "[http://tennesseeencyclopedia.net/entry.php?rec=1285 Don Sundquist]," ''Tennessee Encyclopedia of History and Culture'', 2009. Retrieved: January 9, 2013. In 1996, Sundquist eliminated the state's scandal-ridden [[Tennessee Public Service Commission|Public Service Commission]], replacing it with the [[Tennessee Regulatory Authority]].[http://www.tn.gov/tsla/history/govpapers/findingaids/gp55_with_addn.pdf Governor Don Sundquist Papers (finding aid)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121011162141/http://www.tn.gov/tsla/history/govpapers/findingaids/gp55_with_addn.pdf|date=October 11, 2012}}, Tennessee State Library and Archives, 2007. Retrieved: January 9, 2013. That same year, he created the [[Tennessee Department of Children's Services|Department of Children's Services]].Carroll Van West, "[http://tennesseeencyclopedia.net/entry.php?rec=1285 Don Sundquist]," ''Tennessee Encyclopedia of History and Culture'', 2009. Retrieved: January 9, 2013. == Republican primary == [[Don Sundquist]] easily won the nomination, winning over 80% of the vote in the primary to [[David Y. Copeland III]].[http://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=338048 Our Campaigns – TN Governor, Republican primary, 1994]. Retrieved: January 9, 2013. == Democratic primary == Bredesen won the Democratic nomination for governor, capturing 53% of the vote in a primary that included more than a half-dozen candidates, among them Shelby County Mayor [[William N.
